description:
Mark Zuckerberg's Very Own.

Building an agentic AI gadget to work with astronaut's mental health.
summary:
SansarMind is mental-health support for astronauts in the 13 days between psychologist calls. On the ISS, crew members speak with a psychologist for about 15 minutes every two weeks. NASA notes that astronauts tend to under-report problems, and on a Mars mission a 22-minute signal delay makes live calls impossible.

We built a working prototype with two parts: a wrist gadget (an ESP32-S3 M5Stack StickS3) and a live dashboard for the psychologist. Each morning the astronaut takes about five minutes for a mood and stress check-in, a reaction test based on NASA’s ISS Reaction Self-Test, a sleep score from the wrist motion sensor and optional guided breathing. They can also talk to Sansar, a voice companion powered by Muse AI by Meta. The dashboard compares every result with the astronaut’s own first-week baseline, flags drift early, and gives the psychologist talking points for the next call. Nothing is shared without the astronaut’s consent, except an immediate red flag if they mention harm or danger.

This addresses NASA’s research gap BH-201, which calls for semi-autonomous behavioral health monitoring. The concept hardware costs about $27 a unit, so the same approach could support people on Earth who live far from mental-health care.
details:
What it does and how it works
SansarMind helps astronauts look after their mental health in the 13 days between psychologist calls, and gives the psychologist on Earth an early, honest picture of how each crew member is doing. On the ISS, astronauts speak with a psychologist for about 15 minutes every two weeks. On a Mars mission, a 22-minute signal delay would make live calls impossible.

Each morning the astronaut spends about five minutes with a wrist gadget:

  • a check-in with four questions (mood, stress, sleep quality, connection to crew and family)
  • a reaction test modelled on NASA’s ISS Reaction Self-Test (median reaction time, lapses, false starts)
  • last night’s sleep, scored with the van Hees (2015) arm-angle method
  • optional guided box breathing

They can also hold a button and talk to Sansar, a voice companion powered by Muse AI by Meta. Sansar knows the astronaut’s recent trends, offers one gentle suggestion and never diagnoses. Sansar sums up the day, and the astronaut decides whether to share it. On the psychologist’s dashboard, every result is compared with the astronaut’s own first-week baseline. A yellow flag means a steady drift; a red flag means a safety concern raised with Sansar, which reaches the psychologist immediately.

Benefits

  • Daily, objective data instead of asking someone to remember how the last two weeks went.
  • Problems are spotted days earlier, so the 15-minute call starts with what actually changed.
  • Astronauts control what they share, which builds the trust needed to report honestly.
  • Works offline: results queue on the wrist and upload when a connection returns.

Intended impact
SansarMind targets NASA’s research gap BH-201, which calls for semi-autonomous behavioral health monitoring on Artemis and Mars missions. On Earth, the same low-cost approach could support Antarctic crews, submariners, remote mining camps and rural Mongolian communities far from mental-health care. Our concept device would cost about $27 per unit at 1,000 units.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Hardware: M5Stack StickS3 (ESP32-S3, 8 MB PSRAM, 1.14-inch colour screen, microphone and speaker, BMI270 6-axis motion sensor, two buttons).
  • Firmware: C on the ESP32-S3, including our own reaction-test and sleep-scoring modules.
  • AI: Muse AI by Meta powers Sansar’s conversations; Whisper turns speech into text on the base computer.
  • Web: Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4 and Recharts for the dashboard and the browser simulator, with Supabase (database and Realtime) and Vercel for hosting.
  • Data and testing: Python for generating synthetic astronaut stories, and a Node.js “fake stick” for testing uploads.

How it is creative

  • The gadget’s real firmware screens are ported to run in a web browser, so anyone can try the device at sansarmind.vercel.app.
  • The whole interface works with two buttons, so it can be used with gloves on.
  • The name joins the Mongolian word for space (сансар) with “mind”.

Factors we considered

  • Privacy and consent: nothing is shared without the astronaut pressing Share, except safety red flags. Each device has its own key, and health data never reaches a browser.
  • Scientific validity: we used established methods (PVT-B, van Hees sleep scoring, ecological momentary assessment) and compare each astronaut with their own baseline, not a population average.
  • Safety: Sansar never diagnoses and always points to the psychologist; our next step is a check-in safety question so a red flag never depends on the AI alone.
  • Honest limits: the prototype simulates overnight motion for sleep, and all data shown is demo data. SansarMind is a support tool for clinicians, not a medical device.
